opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest change is that I spend much less time thinking about the model as a thing that answers a question, and much more time thinking about it as a thing that *does work over time*.

When you're building for a chat setting, a lot of your attention goes into the single response. Is it correct, is it well written, is it aligned with what the user wanted. Once you move into an agent setting, that single turn becomes almost a small unit. What matters is whether the model can hold a goal across dozens or hundreds of steps, whether it notices when something went wrong three steps ago, whether it knows when to stop and ask instead of pushing forward confidently. Those are very different capabilities, and frankly a lot of our earlier evaluation habits didn't capture them well.

So my focus shifted in a few ways. First, toward the environment. In an agent framework, the quality of the tools, the feedback signals, and the sandbox matter almost as much as the model itself. If the environment gives noisy or misleading feedback, the model learns the wrong lessons. I used to think of infrastructure as supporting work; now I think of it as part of the research.

Second, toward long-horizon reliability rather than peak capability. A model that is brilliant 90% of the time but makes one unrecoverable mistake in a long task is, in practice, not that useful. So I care a lot more about consistency, error recovery, and the model's ability to check its own work.

And third, toward the human side. When an agent is actually taking actions, the question of when it should defer to a person becomes very concrete. It's no longer a philosophical discussion. You see it immediately: the agent deletes the wrong file, or sends something it shouldn't. That has made me take judgment and calibration much more seriously as core research problems, not just safety add-ons.

If I had to summarize it, I'd say I moved from asking "how smart is the model" to asking "how much can I trust it to work on its own, and how do I know." That second question is harder, but I think it's the one that really matters now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changing research priorities and agent reliability, but does not say that the framework makes the agent’s capabilities less surprising.

r002.rationale: It does not identify imagining what the agent still cannot do as Fuli Luo’s current bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes long-horizon reliability, environment quality, and trust; it does not identify operational efficiency after the agent can perform desired tasks as the focus.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest shift is that I stopped thinking of myself as the person who writes the code, and started thinking of myself as the person who sets the problem.

When we first built the framework with Opus, I expected the gain to be speed. You describe a module, it drafts it, you fix it. And that was real, but it turned out to be the smaller part. The bigger change was that once the agent could run experiments end to end, pull the logs, and come back with a summary, my time went into deciding which questions were worth asking at all. Before, maybe seventy percent of my week was plumbing. Data pipelines, evaluation harnesses, chasing a shape mismatch at two in the morning. Now that work still happens, but I'm not the one doing it, so I'm forced to confront the thing I used to avoid, which is: do I actually know what I'm trying to learn from this run?

The second thing it changed is how I think about taste. When execution is cheap, judgment becomes the bottleneck. Which baselines matter, what counts as a surprising result versus noise, when to stop a direction. Those used to feel like soft skills, almost intuition. Now they're the core of the job, and I spend much more time trying to make that judgment explicit, because I have to write it down for the agent anyway. If I can't articulate why one experiment is more informative than another, the agent can't either.

And the third thing, which I didn't expect, is that it made me more careful, not less. When the agent produces ten plausible analyses a day, you learn quickly that plausible is not the same as true. So a lot of my attention now goes to verification. Building checks the agent can't talk its way around, keeping a small set of experiments I still run by hand so my own intuition doesn't atrophy. I think of it like a pilot who still does manual landings even though autopilot exists.

So if I had to summarize: I focus less on how, and much more on what and why. And on making sure I still understand the system well enough to know when the answer it gives me is wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes the agent running experiments end to end, but does not say its capabilities have become less surprising.

r002.rationale: It identifies choosing worthwhile questions and exercising judgment as bottlenecks, not imagining what the agent still cannot do.

r003.rationale: It says execution is cheap and operational work is handled by the agent, but names deciding what to learn and verifying results as the focus—not improving operational efficiency.

astra-6.text: It’s shifted my focus from the model’s individual answers to how it carries out a whole task. What context does it need? When should it use a tool, and when should it ask for clarification? How does it recognize that something went wrong? With an agent framework, those questions become central. I’m thinking more about the feedback loop—how the system takes an action, observes the result, and adjusts—and how to make that process reliable enough for someone to trust it with real work.

sol-6.1.text: It’s shifted my focus from the model’s individual response to the whole process of getting something done. With an agent framework, you have to think about how the model plans, uses tools, keeps track of context, and recognizes when it needs to correct itself. So I spend more time thinking about the connection between the model and its environment, and how to make that interaction reliable over a longer task.
